h1: Underfloor heating installation in Stoke Poges

hero.intro: Stoke Poges is a village of large plots and substantial houses, with Stoke Park's golf and country club giving the area its best-known identity. The housing ranges from older period detached homes to more recent executive-style builds, many set well back from the road on sizeable gardens, and that range of ages matters as much for underfloor heating as it does for layout.

sections.heading: Period detached homes vs executive-style builds
sections.body: Older period detached houses in Stoke Poges often have a suspended timber bathroom floor — joists and boards over a void rather than a solid slab — particularly where the bathroom sits above an original part of the house. That calls for a careful look at joist condition and span before we fit anything, and we typically run a low-profile electric heating mat over a rigid insulation-backed board across the joists, so heat is pushed up into the room rather than down into the void. The more recent executive-style builds in the village are more likely to be on a solid concrete ground floor, where water-fed underfloor heating screeded over an insulation layer, tied into the central heating, is a straightforward option too.

sections.heading: What Stoke Poges' larger plots mean for the layout around a heated floor
sections.body: That scale generally gives us far more room to manoeuvre on layout than a smaller property would allow — relocating a waste run, widening a doorway for level access, or adding a second en-suite off a principal bedroom rarely runs into the structural constraints a terraced house would present. The same applies when we're fitting underfloor heating: if the floor build-up needs to change levels to suit the system, a larger bathroom and a house with room to adjust a threshold gives us options that a boxed-in terraced bathroom simply doesn't have.

sections.heading: Managing floor height so nothing clashes later
sections.body: Underfloor heating adds height on top of the existing floor — insulation, then the heating element, then screed or board, then tile adhesive and tile. Depending on the system, that's typically 15mm to 70mm in total. We measure this at survey stage against doors, thresholds and any step down into an adjoining room, because getting it wrong means a door that won't close or an uneven transition once the floor is finished and tiled.

sections.heading: From survey to finished floor
sections.body: Once we've confirmed whether your bathroom sits on joists or a slab and agreed the system, we strip the floor back, make good any structural work needed, lay insulation, then the mat or pipe, test it before it's covered, then screed or board over it ahead of tiling. The thermostat is wired, commissioned and tested, and we snag the finished room before handing it back.

faqs.q: Does my period house in Stoke Poges need a different underfloor heating system to a newer build?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Older houses with a suspended timber floor usually suit a low-profile electric mat over an insulation-backed board. Newer executive-style builds on a solid slab can more easily take a screeded water-fed system.

faqs.q: Can underfloor heating be added when we're widening a doorway or changing the layout?
faqs.a: Yes, and the larger plots common in Stoke Poges often give more scope to adjust a threshold or doorway alongside a floor height change than a smaller terraced property would allow.

faqs.q: How much will underfloor heating raise my floor level?
faqs.a: Typically 15mm to 70mm depending on the system, covering insulation, the heating mat or pipe, screed or board, and the tile and adhesive on top. We account for this against doors and thresholds at survey.

faqs.q: Do you check the joists before fitting underfloor heating in an older property?
faqs.a: Yes, always, where the bathroom sits over a suspended timber floor. We check span, spacing and condition before specifying the insulation board and heating mat.
